clinicalPearls: Retinal changes occurring at high altitude, including dilated tortuous vessels, retinal haemorrhages and disc hyperaemia
Most retinal haemorrhages are peripheral and asymptomatic, discovered only on fundoscopy
Visual symptoms occur mainly when a haemorrhage involves the macula
It is part of the spectrum of high-altitude illness and is more likely with higher altitude, rapid ascent and strenuous exertion
Its presence may accompany other altitude illness such as high-altitude cerebral oedema
Descent generally leads to resolution of the haemorrhages over weeks
reference.pathophysiology: High-altitude retinopathy arises from the retinal vascular response to hypobaric hypoxia. Hypoxia causes retinal vasodilatation and increased retinal blood flow, and raised intracranial and venous pressure together with impaired autoregulation predispose the fragile retinal vessels to leak, producing haemorrhages. The same hypoxic and haemodynamic stresses that drive cerebral involvement in severe altitude illness contribute to the retinal findings, so extensive retinopathy can be a marker of significant altitude stress.
additionalDifferentials: Retinal haemorrhage from hypertension or diabetes
Anaemia or blood dyscrasia causing retinal haemorrhage
Optic disc oedema from other causes
additionalInvestigations: Dilated fundus examination documenting haemorrhages and vascular changes
Assessment for other features of altitude illness
Visual acuity testing, particularly for macular involvement
Optical coherence tomography where macular involvement is suspected
Exclusion of systemic causes of retinal haemorrhage
redFlags: Coexisting signs of high-altitude cerebral oedema
reference.prognosis: Peripheral haemorrhages usually resolve completely after descent with no lasting visual effect, though macular involvement can leave persistent visual deficit.
pitfalls: Dismissing extensive retinopathy that may signal serious altitude illness
Attributing haemorrhages to altitude without excluding systemic causes
Overlooking macular involvement in a symptomatic climber
Allowing continued ascent despite significant retinopathy
management: Descent to lower altitude, which allows spontaneous resolution of retinal haemorrhages
Observation of peripheral asymptomatic haemorrhages, which need no specific intervention
Supplemental oxygen as part of treating coexisting altitude illness
Ophthalmology referral and closer monitoring where a haemorrhage involves the macula and threatens vision
Assessment for concurrent high-altitude cerebral or pulmonary oedema
Preventive gradual ascent and avoidance of strenuous exertion in susceptible individuals
Follow-up fundoscopy and visual acuity testing until haemorrhages resolve
